question: How to improve site safety when using robotics?

answer.answer:
Only one cited route leads to Improve site safety (VA13): taking the work off the site altogether through Prefabrication/off-site (PR2), and that link is carried by 12 of the 50 coded cases even though 39 draw on site safety in its own right. Where people must stay beside the machine, Human-robot interaction (CO6) is cited as mitigating Work safety concern (RI20), but on standards evidence and carried by only 4 cases, and it is conditional on two things: Require workforce training (RI6), which 44 of the 50 cases draw on, and Regulatory/legal concern (RI18), meaning compliance with robot safety standards. So the practical advice splits: prefabricate what you can, and for what stays on site treat training and standards compliance as the preconditions rather than the robot itself. Three deployed records in the Japanese census were adopted to address safety, all of them digging, handling or drilling work, which is the removal-of-the-worker-from-the-hazard pattern rather than the collaborative one.

**The one cited path into site safety**

VA13 "Improve site safety" carries 1 inbound and 0 outbound dependency edges, and 39 of the 50 coded cases draw on it. [1] That single inbound edge is PR2 "Prefabrication/off-site" enablesCapability VA13, on the reasoning that moving work offsite improves site safety, backed by peer-reviewed evidence and carried by 12 of the 50 coded cases [1]. 20 of the 50 cases draw on PR2 itself. [1] Everything else attached to VA13 in the retrieved material is co-occurrence, which is correlation and not a claim of cause: VA13 co-occurs with RE6 "Significant human involvement" in 39 cases, with VA2 in 39, with RI6 in 36 [1].

If you take the prefabrication route, its own cited requirements, all peer-reviewed, are organisational as much as technical and they are not equal in weight:

- PR9 "DfMA for DFAB process" enablesCapability PR2, orienting the project toward offsite manufacture, carried by 15 of the 50 [1]; 15 cases draw on PR9 [1].
- CO11 "Early contractor involvement" enablesCapability PR2: manufacturing and assembly knowledge has to enter the design phase, which means selecting a delivery method that brings the producing party in early. Carried by 13 of the 50 [1]; 14 cases draw on CO11 [1].
- VA14 "Integrate supply chain" enablesCapability PR2, carried by 12 of the 50 [1].
- Upstream requirements of PR2 itself: PR2 dependsOn RI14 "Rely on precise planning", carried by 18 of the 50 [1] (36 cases draw on RI14 [1]), and PR2 dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern", where offsite compliance requires third-party certification and traceability, carried by 10 of the 50 [1].
- Where the robot does the assembly, PR4 "Robotic assembly" hasPrecondition PR2: automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials. That edge is carried by only 4 of the 50 [1], and 13 cases draw on PR4 [1].

The pay-off of prefabrication is not safety alone: PR2 enablesCapability VA2 "Reduce time/improve productivity/efficiency", carried by 19 of the 50 [1], VA3 "Improve quality/performance", carried by 18 [1], and VA10 "Reduce errors/constraints", carried by 14 [1]. The safety edge is the least carried of those four.

**Safety for work that stays on site**

CO6 "Human-robot interaction" (Condition) is the anchor here, and its full edge set is three outbound edges:

- CO6 mitigates RI20 "Work safety concern", on the mechanism that power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation within biomechanical limits mitigates contact-injury risk. Evidence is a standard, and the edge is carried by 4 of the 50 coded cases. [1]
- CO6 dependsOn RI6 "Require workforce training": the success of human-robot collaboration is contingent on a skilled workforce. Peer-reviewed, carried by 27 of the 50. [1]
- CO6 dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern", meaning compliance with robot safety standards. Standards evidence, carried by 2 of the 50. [1]

Read the direction carefully: RI6 and RI18 are what CO6 depends on, so training and standards compliance are upstream, to be in place before the collaborative arrangement delivers any mitigation. The asymmetry matters. 44 of the 50 cases draw on RI6 [1], 32 on CO6 [1], 12 on RI18 [1] and 13 on RI20 [1]. RI20 is not an anchor here: it carries 3 cited dependency edges in total, of which only CO6's appears in this material [1], so nothing can be said about how many routes reach it beyond that one.

Two related enablers carry no cited edge at all and so are invisible to any edge-walk, yet are strongly present in the record: CO8 "Remote-control" (Condition) is drawn on by 18 of the 50 cases and carries no dependency edges [1], and VA25 "Reduce disruption due to hazards" (Value) by 13, also with no edges [1]. The literature has not connected either to site safety, but separation of the operator from the hazard is the obvious mechanism and the record supports its presence. Likewise RI9 "Rely on digital system" is drawn on by 39 of the 50 and carries no edge [1], which is the exposure you take on in exchange.

**What the deployed Japanese records show**

Three census records in the context were adopted to address safety, and all three remove the worker from heavy or hazardous operations rather than pairing them with a collaborative robot: census_RXM1-3, adopted to address safety and market, performing digging and material handling on sitework, at technology readiness level 8 [2]; census_RXM4-5, adopted to address safety and labor, performing digging and material handling on sitework, substructure and foundation, at technology readiness level 8 [3]; and census_RXM23-1, adopted to address safety, performing drilling on the structural core and sitework, at technology readiness level 7 [4]. The context gives no firm behind any of the three, and it does not link them to VA13 or to any other enabler, so they evidence the safety motive and the maturity level but not which enablers they draw on.

Note that "robotics" was read across several enablers here, including Robotic drilling (PR19), Robotic pickup/selection (PR15), Gantry-type robotic system (RE10) and Robotic arm (RE2). That widening does not add a safety path: PR19 is drawn on by 9 of the 50 and carries no dependency edges [1], PR15 by 19 with no edges [1], RE10 by 5 with no edges [1], and RE2 "Robotic arm", drawn on by 22, carries only its reciprocal pair with PR4 "Robotic assembly", carried by 12 of the 50 [1]. The machine, in other words, has no cited edge to safety in either direction; the cited routes run through the process choice and the human conditions around it.
